A 44-year-old man was referred to our unit for the revision of 
his spinal cord stimulator following hardware failure. He suffered 
a back injury 14 years ago and subsequently developed severe pain 
in his back and medial right thigh. This evolved into severe, pain-
ful, recurrent spasms of the whole right leg which were refractory 
to physiotherapy, non-steroidals, analgesics and epidural blocks.
  Electromyogram studies confirmed the failure to achieve elec-
trical silence in his right thoracolumbar paraspinal and right tib-
ialis posterior muscles in keeping with a diagnosis of SLS. This 
was labelled as atypical as he exhibited features of both SLS and 
stiff person syndrome (SPS), as well as testing negative for anti-
glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD) antibodies. In 2004, follow-
ing a period of failed conservative management, he underwent a 
percutaneous implantation of a Medtronic /L50128  quadripolar SCS at 
level T 
10–11  which was connected to an implantable pulse genera-
tor (IPG). This device was successful in controlling the pain but he 
continued to experience debilitating spasms related to his SLS.
  He was referred to our unit in 2006 as his pain had returned. 
An interrogation of the SCS device revealed high impedance in 
all 4 contacts confirming hardware failure, and a revision was 
planned. The patient was severely debilitated by the return of his 
pain and also the progression of his spasms. The spasms occurred 
up to 4 times a day precipitated by minor knocks and would last 
between 1 and 4 h. He eventually developed chronic lymphoede-
ma of his right leg that resulted in a fixed inversion of the foot, 
confining him to his house. Pre-operatively his polypharmacy in-
cluded substantial doses of baclofen, benzodiazepines and vari-
ous opioid medications.

During the revision of the hardware it was noted that the pre-
viously implanted electrode had kinked suggesting an insulation 
break at the level of entry into the spine. The electrode was re-
placed at T 
10–11  with a Medtronic Resume TL and the extension 
wire was replaced and connected to the IPG. The stimulator was 
set with the following settings: pulse amplitude 3.0 V, range 0–5.0, 
pulse width 300  /H9262 s, pulse rate 60–130 Hz. As it was noted that the 
patient was only using the upper 2 contacts with the pre-revision 
stimulator, the replacement was positioned slightly more cepha-
lad, physiologically and radiologically midline.
  After the revision the SCS provided excellent coverage of the 
painful limb. During programming and whilst having a spas-
modic episode, it was unexpectedly noted that a high amplitude 
current with a wide pulse width could abort his spasms. The fol-
low-up 6 weeks later revealed that the patient was in fact using his 
stimulator to abort his spasmodic episodes more than for his pri-
mary indication of pain.
  At 1 year after the revision, his lymphoedema had completely 
resolved, the analgesia and benzodiazepine dependence had sig-
nificantly improved and more importantly his quality of life had 
improved. He was now able to mobilise with the use of 1 crutch 
and reach his local restaurant 150 yards away. He was also able to 
abort his spasm within 1 min of onset. He is due to see a pain spe-
cialist with a view to completely stopping all opiates.

I n  o u r  r e p o r t  a  n u m b e r  o f  o b s e r v a t i o n s  w e r e  m a d e  
with respect to the abortion of the spasms:
  – The anti-spasmodic effect was only observed when the 
SCS was programmed to a higher current (ampere) 
with a wide pulse width (above 210 /H9262s). It is known 
that the physical effect of a wide pulse width and a high 
ampere current from a midline dorsally placed epidu-
ral electrode has greater and deeper recruitment of the 
spinal cord area in the current field. However, research 
has shown that in clinical situations the deeper and 
more ventral recruitment is unlikely to spread to the 
ventral motor tracts  
[11] .

Fig. 2.  The spinal cord also contains neuronal circuits called cen-
tral pattern generators. These generate co-ordinated rhythmic 
flexion and extension of the limbs allowing functionally complete 
walking and running movements. Interneurones are vital to this 
function. Adapted with permission from Dr. R.E. Burke  
[16] .

– The effect was rapid and cumulative but not instanta-
neous. The spasmodic episode was aborted as the 
spasm frequency and strength slowly decayed. In total 
it took approximately 80 s for the spasm to be aborted 
with the SCS, compared with the natural resolution 
time of anywhere between 1 and 4 h. This dramatic 
ability to arrest the spasm promptly has significantly 
improved the patient’s quality of life. 
 – No SCS-related aberrant motor activity was noted 
during up-programming of the ampere or afterwards. 
 – The patient did not feel any unpleasant sensation/pain 
when the higher current (ampere) was applied. In nor-
mal subjects high currents and wide pulse widths 
would probably produce unwanted effects. 
 – The anti-spasmodic effects outlasted the high current 
stimulation period such that post-stimulation and 
further exterostimulation did not provoke spasms. 
 – Switching off the stimulator brought about a return of 
the symptoms within a few hours suggesting that im-
provement of the symptoms with the SCS was not re-
lated to the natural history of the disease.

Conclusion 
 Though the mechanism is speculative, SCS may be-
come a useful adjunct in the management of intractable 
spasms associated with SLS. However, as this is the only 
case, further trials with careful selection and individu-
alisation of the stimulation parameters are indicated.
